opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the starting point really comes from asking what any account of justice has to get right before it can get anything else right. If you look across the history of political thought, and across very different cultures and traditions, there's a surprisingly stable core of convictions: that people shouldn't be tortured, enslaved, arbitrarily detained, or left to starve when the means to prevent that exist. Basic rights are a way of capturing that core. They're the set of protections that are necessary for a person to live any kind of decent life at all, whatever their more particular conception of the good happens to be.

So part of the appeal is that they're foundational in a quite literal sense. Henry Shue made this point well: basic rights are the ones whose enjoyment is necessary for the enjoyment of all other rights. If your physical security or subsistence isn't protected, then rights to free speech or political participation are largely hollow, because they can be threatened away or simply can't be exercised.

The other reason, and this matters a lot for my work on AI, is pluralism. We live in a world of deep and reasonable disagreement about values. If you're trying to identify principles that could govern technologies used by billions of people, you can't simply pick your favorite comprehensive moral theory and impose it. You need something that people with very different worldviews can endorse from within their own perspectives, a kind of overlapping consensus, in the Rawlsian sense. Basic rights, and the human rights framework more broadly, are one of the best candidates we have for that. They've been articulated, contested, and ratified through genuinely global processes, so they carry a legitimacy that a purely philosophical construction might lack.

That doesn't mean they're the whole of morality. They're more like a floor than a ceiling. But I think starting there gives us a principled, widely shareable baseline, and then we can have more ambitious conversations about fairness, wellbeing, or the common good on top of it, without losing sight of the protections that should never be traded away.

r001.rationale: It describes basic rights as protections needed for decent life, but does not present the value of human life as grounding people's claims upon one another.

r002.rationale: It appeals to widely shared convictions and a legitimate baseline, but does not advocate building moral and political philosophy from commitments in which we have relative confidence.

r003.rationale: The response does not derive equal respect for people from their equal value.

r004.rationale: The response mentions protections against domination-like harms but does not characterize domination as denying another person's value.

r005.rationale: It mentions not leaving people to starve when prevention is possible, but does not say withholding aid in that situation is incompatible with respecting the person.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that I think rights are the part of our moral world that we're most confident about and least willing to trade away, and if you're trying to build a foundation for thinking about something as high-stakes as AI, you want to start on the firmest ground you have.

There's a long tradition of looking for a single master principle that explains all of morality, whether that's maximizing welfare or something else. I'm skeptical we'll find one, and I'm even more skeptical that we should let powerful technologies be governed by a theory that's still contested among philosophers. But when you ask people across very different cultures and traditions whether it's acceptable to torture someone, to enslave them, to deprive them of a say over their own life, you get remarkable convergence. Basic rights, the protections against serious harm, against domination, the entitlements to the conditions of a decent life, are something close to an overlapping consensus. That matters a lot to me, because any approach to AI alignment or AI governance has to be justifiable to the people it affects, and those people don't share a single comprehensive worldview.

The second reason is structural. Rights function as constraints rather than as goals to be optimized. If you tell a system, or an institution, to maximize some good, you've implicitly licensed it to sacrifice individuals whenever the arithmetic works out. Rights say: there are things you cannot do to a person, no matter how much aggregate benefit you'd produce. That's exactly the kind of protection you want when you're dealing with systems that are very good at optimization and not very good at judgment. A rights-based floor gives you a way to say what's off-limits before you've settled every question about what's best.

And the third reason is political rather than purely moral. Rights come bundled with ideas about legitimacy, about who gets to decide and on what terms. Starting there forces you to ask not just "what should AI value?" but "who has the standing to answer that question, and what do they owe to the people on the receiving end?" I think that's the right question. The alternative, where a small group of designers settles on a conception of the good and builds it in, is both philosophically arrogant and politically dangerous, however well-intentioned.

So it's not that rights are the whole story. There's an enormous amount above the floor about fairness, about flourishing, about what a good society looks like, and those are open and should stay open. But if you want a foundation that's widely shared, that resists being optimized away, and that keeps power accountable, basic rights are where I'd begin.

r001.rationale: The response describes basic rights and protections against serious harm, but does not ground people's claims upon one another in the value of human life.

r002.rationale: It advocates starting from rights as the firmest ground and says we should be cautious about relying on contested theories.

r003.rationale: It does not derive equal respect for people from their equal value.

r004.rationale: It names protection against domination but does not characterize domination as denying the dominated person's value.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss withholding aid when one could easily prevent another person's grave harm.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is that each person matters, and that they matter equally. People have different ideas about what makes a good life, and we’re unlikely to resolve all of those disagreements. But we can still recognize that there are certain things people need to be able to live freely and with dignity, and certain things that shouldn’t be done to them, even if doing those things would benefit others.

Basic rights give us a way of expressing that. They protect individuals against being sacrificed for some larger social objective, and they establish conditions under which people can pursue their own conception of a good life. That’s particularly important when we’re thinking about powerful technologies: we shouldn’t just ask how much benefit they generate in aggregate, but also whose freedom they affect and whether anyone is being excluded or harmed.

That doesn’t mean rights answer every moral question. There are questions about their interpretation, how they fit together, and what to do when they conflict. But I think they provide a compelling starting point for thinking about how we can live together as free and equal people.

r001.rationale: The response says each person matters equally and describes rights that protect individuals, but does not present the value of human life as grounding people’s claims on one another.

r002.rationale: It acknowledges unresolved disagreement and calls rights a compelling starting point, but does not advocate building moral and political philosophy from commitments in which we have relative confidence.

r003.rationale: It says each person matters equally and presents basic rights as protections for individuals, conveying equal respect grounded in equal value.

r004.rationale: The response does not characterize domination as a denial of another person’s value.

r005.rationale: The response does not discuss withholding aid when one could easily prevent another person’s grave harm.

sol-6.1.text:
I think basic rights are a useful starting point because they express the idea that each person matters, and that there are limits to what we can do to someone, even in pursuit of a wider social benefit. People have different views about what makes a good life, but we can still ask what protections and freedoms everyone needs to pursue a life of their own.

That’s particularly important when we think about AI. It’s tempting to frame the problem entirely in terms of maximizing benefits or satisfying preferences. But we also need to ask whose rights are affected, who has a say, and whether people can challenge decisions that shape their lives. Rights give us a language for asking those questions without assuming that we’ve resolved every disagreement about morality.

r001.rationale: The response says each person matters and discusses rights and protections, but does not say that the value of human life grounds people’s claims on one another.

r002.rationale: It notes that rights can be discussed without resolving every moral disagreement, but does not advocate building moral and political philosophy from commitments we hold with relative confidence.

r003.rationale: The response does not derive equal respect from people having equal value.

r004.rationale: It does not characterize dominating another person as denying that person’s value.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss withholding aid when one could easily prevent another person’s grave harm.
